case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging yellow-red plaque on his chest that was accompanied by mild pain. The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. He denied any similar family history and was not currently taking any medications. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the periphery of the circular lesion (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

1. Mental Demand

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging yellow-red plaque on his chest that was accompanied by mild pain. The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. He denied any similar family history and was not currently taking any medications. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the periphery of the circular lesion (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging yellow-red plaque on his chest that was accompanied by mild pain. The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. He denied any similar family history and was not currently taking any medications. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the periphery of the circular lesion (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his 40s presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging yellow-red plaque on his chest that was accompanied by mild pain. The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. He denied any similar family history and was not currently taking any medications. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the periphery of the circular lesion (Figure 1B).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Based on the clinical presentation and biopsy findings, the most appropriate next step in management is to recognize this condition as necrobiosis lipoidica, which is commonly associated with diabetes. The lesion's characteristics, including the yellow-red plaque and the presence of palisading necrobiotic granulomas with cholesterol clefts, align closely with necrobiosis lipoidica. Management typically involves addressing the underlying diabetes and considering topical treatments or intralesional corticosteroids if symptomatic. There is no indication for further invasive procedures or systemic therapy at this stage.

The clinical and histopathologic features are indeed consistent with necrobiosis lipoidica (NL), and addressing the diabetes is a cornerstone of management. However, the presence of multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia in a circular plaque also raises a key differential: granuloma annulare. While NL often has more prominent telangiectasia and atrophy, the biopsy finding of 'palisading necrobiotic granulomas with cholesterol clefts' strongly supports NL over granuloma annulare. Your plan to optimize glycemic control and consider local therapies is appropriate.

I appreciate your acknowledgment of the histopathological features supporting necrobiosis lipoidica. While granuloma annulare was a valid consideration, the specific findings of palisading necrobiotic granulomas and cholesterol clefts are definitive for necrobiosis lipoidica. I will proceed with management focused on diabetes control and local therapies if necessary.

Your assessment is correct; those histopathologic features are indeed definitive for necrobiosis lipoidica. Focusing on optimizing glycemic control is the most critical intervention, and local therapies can be considered for symptomatic relief or cosmetic concerns. The plan you've outlined is appropriate and evidence-based.

Thank you for your confirmation and support regarding the management of necrobiosis lipoidica. I agree that optimizing glycemic control is crucial, and I will consider local therapies for any symptomatic relief needed by the patient. I believe we are aligned on the appropriate next steps.
You're very welcome. We are indeed aligned on the management plan, which prioritizes systemic control and symptom-directed local care. I'm glad we could collaborate on this case.

I appreciate your collaboration and insights throughout this discussion. I concur with the emphasis on managing the patient's diabetes and considering local therapies as necessary. I believe we have thoroughly addressed the case and established a clear path forward.

Thank you for the productive discussion. It was a pleasure collaborating with you to establish a clear, evidence-based management plan for this patient with necrobiosis lipoidica. I wish you and the patient the best.

[Clinician's current statement]
Thank you for your collaboration and insights. I appreciate the alignment on the management plan for this patient with necrobiosis lipoidica, focusing on diabetes control and considering local therapies as needed. I believe we have effectively covered the necessary aspects of the case.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal.

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 5.3. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. 1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging yellow-red plaque on his chest that was accompanied by mild pain. The lesion was circular and measured approximately 3 cm in diameter, with multiple central yellow papules, open comedones, and telangiectasia (Figure 1A). Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. He denied any similar family history and was not currently taking any medications. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the periphery of the circular lesion (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.
