Further examination revealed no similar lesions on the face, including the periorbital area, or on the limbs, and there was no ocular involvement. The patient had uncontrolled diabetes. He denied any similar family history and was not currently taking any medications. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the periphery of the circular lesion (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Circular yellow-red plaque on the anterior chest, with foci of yellowish color and open comedones. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows numerous palisading necrobiotic granulomas involving the whole dermis; cholesterol clefts can be appreciated (bar = 500 μm).
case_info.explanation: The skin biopsy results revealed hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, atrophy of the spinous layer, and palisading granulomas forming throughout the dermis (Figure 1B). In the central area, degenerated collagen fibers with numerous cholesterol clefts were observed that were surrounded by foamy histiocytes, epithelioid cells, and Touton giant cells, as well as lymphocytes and plasma cells (Figure 2). A diagnosis of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (NXG) was established. The patient opted not to undergo a bone marrow biopsy. Laboratory examination yielded normal results for complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation electrophoresis, lipid panel, and complement levels (C3 and C4). Additionally, ultrasonography imaging of the heart, liver, and spleen showed no substantial abnormalities. The patient was prescribed a topical corticosteroid cream. On 2-week follow-up, the lesion became flattened. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to undergo regular monitoring. NXG is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis commonly linked with paraproteinemia originating from plasma cell dyscrasias or lymphoproliferative disorders. The classic NXG lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, indurated papule, nodule, or plaque displaying a yellowish xanthomatous appearance.1These papules and nodules often merge and form indurated plaques, with superficial telangiectasias and scarring.2Typically, NXG presents with multiple cutaneous lesions that are predominantly located in the periorbital area.3Lesions can also occur on the face, trunk, extremities, and within scars.4The eye represents the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement.4Paraproteinemia is detected in approximately 80% of patients, with immunoglobulin G–κ being the most prevalent subtype.3Histopathologically, NXG exhibits large, palisading, necrobiotic granulomas involving the dermis and often the subcutaneous tissue. Necrobiosis areas are surrounded by granulomas with foreign body–type appearance, foamy histiocytes, and Touton giant cells. Degenerated collagen and cholesterol clefts within necrobiosis are distinctive features.4The diagnosis of NXG relies on a combination of typical clinical features and pathological findings. Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) represents a differential diagnosis for NXG. NL is a rare condition that predominantly affects female individuals. Onset commonly presents during the third decade for individuals with type 1 diabetes and the fourth decade for those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes.5Clinically, NXG and NL may exhibit similar appearances. NL lesions typically initiate as asymptomatic papules or nodules with erythematous borders that merge into violaceous plaques. The central region transitions from red-brown to yellow-brown, often displaying atrophic, waxy, and eroded features. Telangiectasias may form due to underlying collagen degeneration. NL usually localizes to the bilateral lower extremities, with potential occurrence on the face, scalp, trunk, groin, and upper extremities. Histologically, NXG and NL lesions display confluent areas of necrobiosis. However, NXG is characterized by atypical foreign body giant cells and a relatively greater number of Touton cells compared with NL, while lacking vessel hyalinization.6 Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis is a rare reactive granulomatous dermatitis associated with autoimmune connective tissue diseases, lymphoproliferative disorders, and infections. Clinical presentation includes erythematous papules that may ulcerate, umbilicate, or develop a yellowish crust. The lesions are typically symmetrical and involve the elbows and hands.7Histologically, early palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis lesions exhibit neutrophilic infiltrates and leukocytoclastic vasculitis, while fully developed lesions are characterized by palisaded granulomas with degenerating collagen and neutrophil remnants.7 Sarcoidosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting multiple systems, with an unknown etiology. The lungs are the most affected organ in sarcoidosis. Other organs commonly involved include the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes.8Cutaneous manifestations primarily affect the head and neck (including the face) and may also manifest in areas of scars and tattoos.9The most common clinical lesions are erythematous to violaceous infiltrated papules on the face and widely distributed erythematous to violaceous plaques that occur more commonly on the trunk and extremities.8Histologically, these lesions exhibit characteristic noncaseating granulomas comprising densely packed epithelioid macrophages with relatively mild lymphocytic inflammation.9Substantial alterations in collage and the presence of cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells, and palisading granulomas are typically absent in cases of sarcoidosis.10 This case report describes a unique instance of NXG in a patient without paraproteinemia or periorbital lesions. In clinical practice, when observing a yellowish xanthomatous appearance in unconventional sites, comprehensive skin pathology and hematological evaluations that encompass serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis should be considered.
